title: Chain Customer, Order, and Item Details
description_markdown: Join `orders`, `order_items`, and `products`. Return `o.order_id`, `p.product_name`, and `oi.quantity`. Order by `o.order_id` ASC, `p.product_name` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Chain joins across 3 tables
SELECT o.order_id, p.product_name, oi.quantity
FROM orders o
JOIN ...
solution_query: SELECT o.order_id, p.product_name, oi.quantity FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id ORDER BY o.order_id ASC, p.product_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Joins orders to order_items on order_id, then order_items to products on product_id.
hints: Query: SELECT o.order_id, p.product_name, oi.quantity FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id ORDER BY o.order_id ASC, p.product_name ASC;

title: Student Academic Performance Across Tables
description_markdown: Join `students`, `enrollments`, `courses`, and `marks`. Filter for assessment_type = 'final'. Return `s.first_name`, `c.course_code`, and `m.score AS final_score`. Order by `s.first_name` ASC, `c.course_code` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Join students -> enrollments -> courses -> marks
SELECT ...
solution_query: SELECT s.first_name, c.course_code, m.score AS final_score FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id JOIN courses c ON e.course_id = c.course_id JOIN marks m ON e.enrollment_id = m.enrollment_id WHERE m.assessment_type = 'final' ORDER BY s.first_name ASC, c.course_code ASC;
solution_explanation: Traverses a 4-table relational hierarchy to connect student records with their final grades.
hints: Follow the FK relationships: student -> enrollment -> course and enrollment -> marks.
Focus on the required WHERE, JOIN, or GROUP BY clause conditions.

Query: SELECT s.first_name, c.course_code, m.score AS final_score FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id JOIN courses c ON e.course_id = c.course_id JOIN marks m ON e.enrollment_id = m.enrollment_id WHERE m.assessment_type = 'final' ORDER BY s.first_name ASC, c.course_code ASC;

title: Aggregate Employee Project Assignment Workloads
description_markdown: Join `employees`, `assignments`, and `projects`. For each employee who has assignments, calculate the count of distinct projects worked (`COUNT(DISTINCT a.project_id)` as `project_count`) and total hours (`SUM(a.hours_worked)` as `total_hours`). Return `e.first_name`, `project_count`, and `total_hours`. Order by `total_hours` DESC, `e.emp_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Multi-table join with GROUP BY
SELECT ...
solution_query: SELECT e.first_name, COUNT(DISTINCT a.project_id) AS project_count, SUM(a.hours_worked) AS total_hours FROM employees e JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id JOIN projects p ON a.project_id = p.project_id GROUP BY e.emp_id, e.first_name ORDER BY total_hours DESC, e.emp_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Joins assignments to projects and employees while aggregating project allocations.
hints: Focus on the required WHERE, JOIN, or GROUP BY clause conditions.

Query: SELECT e.first_name, COUNT(DISTINCT a.project_id) AS project_count, SUM(a.hours_worked) AS total_hours FROM employees e JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id JOIN projects p ON a.project_id = p.project_id GROUP BY e.emp_id, e.first_name ORDER BY total_hours DESC, e.emp_id ASC;

title: Link Customers to Products via Order Lines
description_markdown: Join `customers`, `orders`, `order_items`, and `products` on their respective foreign keys. Return `c.first_name`, `o.order_id`, `p.product_name`, and `oi.quantity`. Order by `o.order_id` ascending, then `p.product_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Multi-table join: customers -> orders -> order_items -> products
SELECT c.first_name, o.order_id, p.product_name, oi.quantity
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON ...
JOIN order_items oi ON ...
JOIN products p ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.first_name, o.order_id, p.product_name, oi.quantity FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id ORDER BY o.order_id ASC, p.product_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Chains four tables from customer through order and item details to the physical catalog product name.
common_mistakes: Joining products directly to orders instead of through order_items.
interview_tip: In normalized relational schemas, transaction headers (orders) always connect to items (products) via line items.
hints: Query: SELECT c.first_name, o.order_id, p.product_name, oi.quantity FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id ORDER BY o.order_id ASC, p.product_name ASC;

title: Verify Customer Payment Methods and Amounts
description_markdown: Join `customers`, `orders`, and `payments`. Return `c.email`, `o.order_id`, `pay.payment_method`, and `pay.amount`. Order results by `o.order_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Multi-table join: customers -> orders -> payments
SELECT c.email, o.order_id, pay.payment_method, pay.amount
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON ...
JOIN payments pay ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.email, o.order_id, pay.payment_method, pay.amount FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN payments pay ON o.order_id = pay.order_id ORDER BY o.order_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Links customer identity to processed financial settlement transactions via order records.
common_mistakes: Joining payments directly to customers without passing through orders.
interview_tip: Trace the primary-foreign key path carefully across entity relationship boundaries.
hints: Query: SELECT c.email, o.order_id, pay.payment_method, pay.amount FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN payments pay ON o.order_id = pay.order_id ORDER BY o.order_id ASC;

title: Track Category Merchandise Orders
description_markdown: Join `categories`, `products`, and `order_items`. Return `c.category_name`, `p.product_name`, and `oi.order_id`. Order by `c.category_name` ascending, `p.product_name` ascending, then `oi.order_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Join categories -> products -> order_items
SELECT c.category_name, p.product_name, oi.order_id
FROM categories c
JOIN products p ON ...
JOIN order_items oi ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.category_name, p.product_name, oi.order_id FROM categories c JOIN products p ON c.category_id = p.category_id JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id ORDER BY c.category_name ASC, p.product_name ASC, oi.order_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Connects product category classifications down to the individual order item transactions.
common_mistakes: Inverting the join condition on category_id.
interview_tip: Always alias tables clearly (c for categories, p for products, oi for order_items).
hints: Order by `c.category_name ASC, p.product_name ASC, oi.order_id ASC`.

Query: SELECT c.category_name, p.product_name, oi.order_id FROM categories c JOIN products p ON c.category_id = p.category_id JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id ORDER BY c.category_name ASC, p.product_name ASC, oi.order_id ASC;

title: Connect Reviewers with High-Rating Products
description_markdown: Join `customers`, `reviews`, and `products`. Filter for reviews where `r.rating >= 4`. Return `c.first_name`, `p.product_name`, and `r.rating`. Order by `c.first_name` ascending, then `p.product_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Join customers -> reviews -> products
SELECT c.first_name, p.product_name, r.rating
FROM customers c
JOIN reviews r ON ...
JOIN products p ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.first_name, p.product_name, r.rating FROM customers c JOIN reviews r ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id JOIN products p ON r.product_id = p.product_id WHERE r.rating >= 4 ORDER BY c.first_name ASC, p.product_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Bridges user accounts and product catalog items via the reviews junction table.
common_mistakes: Filtering in HAVING without any GROUP BY.
interview_tip: WHERE filters rows before processing; keep rating filtering in WHERE.
hints: Query: SELECT c.first_name, p.product_name, r.rating FROM customers c JOIN reviews r ON c.customer_id = r.customer_id JOIN products p ON r.product_id = p.product_id WHERE r.rating >= 4 ORDER BY c.first_name ASC, p.product_name ASC;

title: Inspect Order Lines Enriched with Category Taxonomy
description_markdown: Join `orders`, `order_items`, `products`, and `categories`. Return `o.order_id`, `p.product_name`, `c.category_name`, and `oi.unit_price`. Order by `o.order_id` ascending, then `p.product_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Join 4 tables: orders -> order_items -> products -> categories
SELECT o.order_id, p.product_name, c.category_name, oi.unit_price
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON ...
JOIN products p ON ...
JOIN categories c ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT o.order_id, p.product_name, c.category_name, oi.unit_price FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id ORDER BY o.order_id ASC, p.product_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Enriches purchased merchandise items with upstream taxonomic category metadata.
common_mistakes: Selecting p.price instead of the charged oi.unit_price.
interview_tip: Always distinguish historical snapshot values (oi.unit_price) from current master data (p.price).
hints: Query: SELECT o.order_id, p.product_name, c.category_name, oi.unit_price FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id JOIN categories c ON p.category_id = c.category_id ORDER BY o.order_id ASC, p.product_name ASC;

title: Filter Verified Customer Payments
description_markdown: Join `customers`, `orders`, and `payments`. Filter where `pay.payment_status = 'success'`. Return `c.first_name`, `c.last_name`, `o.order_id`, and `pay.payment_method`. Order by `c.last_name` ascending, then `o.order_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Join customers -> orders -> payments with filter
SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, o.order_id, pay.payment_method
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON ...
JOIN payments pay ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, o.order_id, pay.payment_method FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN payments pay ON o.order_id = pay.order_id WHERE pay.payment_status = 'success' ORDER BY c.last_name ASC, o.order_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Reconciles customer contact records with successful transactions across the orders bridge table.
common_mistakes: Filtering order_status instead of payment_status.
interview_tip: In payment gateways, transactions can fail while orders remain in draft status; check pay.payment_status.
hints: Query: SELECT c.first_name, c.last_name, o.order_id, pay.payment_method FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN payments pay ON o.order_id = pay.order_id WHERE pay.payment_status = 'success' ORDER BY c.last_name ASC, o.order_id ASC;

title: Join Department Staff with Department Initiatives
description_markdown: Join `employees` and `departments` on `dept_id`, then join `departments` to `projects` on `dept_id`. Return `e.first_name`, `d.dept_name`, and `p.project_name`. Order by `d.dept_name` ascending, `e.first_name` ascending, then `p.project_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Join employees, departments, and projects
SELECT e.first_name, d.dept_name, p.project_name
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON ...
JOIN projects p ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT e.first_name, d.dept_name, p.project_name FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, e.first_name ASC, p.project_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Hub-and-spoke join where departments acts as the central hub connecting employee personnel to department projects.
common_mistakes: Trying to join employees directly to projects without assignments.
interview_tip: Hub-and-spoke schemas use a common parent entity (departments) to connect sibling child tables.
hints: Order by `d.dept_name ASC, e.first_name ASC, p.project_name ASC`.

Query: SELECT e.first_name, d.dept_name, p.project_name FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, e.first_name ASC, p.project_name ASC;

title: Audit Employee Project Staffing and Commitments
description_markdown: Join `employees`, `assignments`, and `projects`. Return `e.first_name`, `e.last_name`, `p.project_name`, `a.role`, and `a.hours_worked`. Order by `p.project_name` ascending, then `e.last_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Join employees -> assignments -> projects
SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name, p.project_name, a.role, a.hours_worked
FROM employees e
JOIN assignments a ON ...
JOIN projects p ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name, p.project_name, a.role, a.hours_worked FROM employees e JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id JOIN projects p ON a.project_id = p.project_id ORDER BY p.project_name ASC, e.last_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Traverses a many-to-many relationship using the assignments junction table.
common_mistakes: Joining on dept_id instead of project_id.
interview_tip: Junction tables with additional payload attributes (like role and hours_worked) are called associative entities.
hints: Query: SELECT e.first_name, e.last_name, p.project_name, a.role, a.hours_worked FROM employees e JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id JOIN projects p ON a.project_id = p.project_id ORDER BY p.project_name ASC, e.last_name ASC;

title: Audit Departmental Salary Adjustments Over Time
description_markdown: Join `departments`, `employees`, and `salaries_history`. Return `d.dept_name`, `e.first_name`, `sh.effective_date`, and `sh.salary`. Order by `d.dept_name` ascending, `e.first_name` ascending, then `sh.effective_date` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Join departments -> employees -> salaries_history
SELECT d.dept_name, e.first_name, sh.effective_date, sh.salary
FROM departments d
JOIN employees e ON ...
JOIN salaries_history sh ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, e.first_name, sh.effective_date, sh.salary FROM departments d JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id JOIN salaries_history sh ON e.emp_id = sh.emp_id ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, e.first_name ASC, sh.effective_date ASC;
solution_explanation: Traces historic pay increases up through the departmental organizational structure.
common_mistakes: Selecting e.salary instead of the historical sh.salary.
interview_tip: Always confirm which table owns the requested metrics in audit queries.
hints: Order by `d.dept_name ASC, e.first_name ASC, sh.effective_date ASC`.

Query: SELECT d.dept_name, e.first_name, sh.effective_date, sh.salary FROM departments d JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id JOIN salaries_history sh ON e.emp_id = sh.emp_id ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, e.first_name ASC, sh.effective_date ASC;

title: Inspect Department Projects and Assigned Staff IDs
description_markdown: Join `departments`, `projects`, and `assignments`. Return `d.dept_name`, `p.project_name`, `a.emp_id`, and `a.hours_worked`. Order by `d.dept_name` ascending, `p.project_name` ascending, then `a.emp_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Join departments -> projects -> assignments
SELECT d.dept_name, p.project_name, a.emp_id, a.hours_worked
FROM departments d
JOIN projects p ON ...
JOIN assignments a ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, p.project_name, a.emp_id, a.hours_worked FROM departments d JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id JOIN assignments a ON p.project_id = a.project_id ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, p.project_name ASC, a.emp_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Tracks project labor hours by department ownership.
common_mistakes: Joining assignments on dept_id instead of project_id.
interview_tip: Notice how foreign keys create a clean, directed acyclic graph across tables.
hints: Order by `d.dept_name ASC, p.project_name ASC, a.emp_id ASC`.

Query: SELECT d.dept_name, p.project_name, a.emp_id, a.hours_worked FROM departments d JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id JOIN assignments a ON p.project_id = a.project_id ORDER BY d.dept_name ASC, p.project_name ASC, a.emp_id ASC;

title: Connect Faculty to Enrolled Student Rosters
description_markdown: Join `professors`, `courses`, and `enrollments`. Return `p.last_name`, `c.course_name`, `e.student_id`, and `e.semester`. Order by `p.last_name` ascending, `c.course_name` ascending, then `e.student_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Join professors -> courses -> enrollments
SELECT p.last_name, c.course_name, e.student_id, e.semester
FROM professors p
JOIN courses c ON ...
JOIN enrollments e ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT p.last_name, c.course_name, e.student_id, e.semester FROM professors p JOIN courses c ON p.professor_id = c.professor_id JOIN enrollments e ON c.course_id = e.course_id ORDER BY p.last_name ASC, c.course_name ASC, e.student_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Maps instructors to student course enrollment rosters across the curriculum.
common_mistakes: Joining enrollments directly to professors.
interview_tip: Enrollments belong to courses; courses belong to professors.
hints: Order by `p.last_name ASC, c.course_name ASC, e.student_id ASC`.

Query: SELECT p.last_name, c.course_name, e.student_id, e.semester FROM professors p JOIN courses c ON p.professor_id = c.professor_id JOIN enrollments e ON c.course_id = e.course_id ORDER BY p.last_name ASC, c.course_name ASC, e.student_id ASC;

title: Retrieve High-Scoring Students Across Assessment Marks
description_markdown: Join `students`, `enrollments`, and `marks`. Filter where `m.score >= 90`. Return `s.first_name`, `s.last_name`, `m.assessment_type`, and `m.score`. Order by `m.score` descending, then `s.last_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Join students -> enrollments -> marks
SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, m.assessment_type, m.score
FROM students s
JOIN enrollments e ON ...
JOIN marks m ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, m.assessment_type, m.score FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id JOIN marks m ON e.enrollment_id = m.enrollment_id WHERE m.score >= 90 ORDER BY m.score DESC, s.last_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Retrieves honor roll student scores through the enrollment bridge table.
common_mistakes: Trying to join marks directly to students without enrollments.
interview_tip: Always follow the relational schema foreign keys: students -> enrollments -> marks.
hints: Query: SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, m.assessment_type, m.score FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id JOIN marks m ON e.enrollment_id = m.enrollment_id WHERE m.score >= 90 ORDER BY m.score DESC, s.last_name ASC;

title: Catalog Student Enrollments by Course Code
description_markdown: Join `courses`, `enrollments`, and `students`. Return `c.course_code`, `s.first_name`, `s.last_name`, and `e.semester`. Order by `c.course_code` ascending, `s.last_name` ascending, then `s.first_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Join courses -> enrollments -> students
SELECT c.course_code, s.first_name, s.last_name, e.semester
FROM courses c
JOIN enrollments e ON ...
JOIN students s ON ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.course_code, s.first_name, s.last_name, e.semester FROM courses c JOIN enrollments e ON c.course_id = e.course_id JOIN students s ON e.student_id = s.student_id ORDER BY c.course_code ASC, s.last_name ASC, s.first_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Constructs an academic class roster by joining courses through enrollments to students.
common_mistakes: Omitting the secondary tie-breaker in ORDER BY.
interview_tip: Rosters and class schedules are canonical examples of many-to-many relationship traversal.
hints: Order by `c.course_code ASC, s.last_name ASC, s.first_name ASC`.

Query: SELECT c.course_code, s.first_name, s.last_name, e.semester FROM courses c JOIN enrollments e ON c.course_id = e.course_id JOIN students s ON e.student_id = s.student_id ORDER BY c.course_code ASC, s.last_name ASC, s.first_name ASC;

title: Audit Final Exam Scores Across Faculty Courses
description_markdown: Join `professors`, `courses`, `enrollments`, and `marks`. Filter for `m.assessment_type = 'final'`. Return `p.last_name`, `c.course_code`, and `m.score`. Order by `p.last_name` ascending, `c.course_code` ascending, then `m.score` descending.
starter_query:
-- Join 4 tables: professors -> courses -> enrollments -> marks
SELECT p.last_name, c.course_code, m.score
FROM professors p
JOIN courses c ON ...
JOIN enrollments e ON ...
JOIN marks m ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT p.last_name, c.course_code, m.score FROM professors p JOIN courses c ON p.professor_id = c.professor_id JOIN enrollments e ON c.course_id = e.course_id JOIN marks m ON e.enrollment_id = m.enrollment_id WHERE m.assessment_type = 'final' ORDER BY p.last_name ASC, c.course_code ASC, m.score DESC;
solution_explanation: Chains four tables from instructor through course and enrollment to final exam mark scores.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the assessment_type = 'final' filter.
interview_tip: In four-table joins, keeping filters tight in WHERE helps the query engine execute fast index scans.
hints: Query: SELECT p.last_name, c.course_code, m.score FROM professors p JOIN courses c ON p.professor_id = c.professor_id JOIN enrollments e ON c.course_id = e.course_id JOIN marks m ON e.enrollment_id = m.enrollment_id WHERE m.assessment_type = 'final' ORDER BY p.last_name ASC, c.course_code ASC, m.score DESC;

title: Calculate Customer Spend Broken Down by Category
description_markdown: Join `customers`, `orders`, `order_items`, `products`, and `categories`. Filter for orders where `o.order_status = 'completed'`. Group by `c.customer_id`, `c.first_name`, `cat.category_id`, and `cat.category_name`. Return `c.first_name`, `cat.category_name`, and `SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS category_spend`. Order by `category_spend` descending, `c.first_name` ascending, `cat.category_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- 5-table join aggregation
SELECT c.first_name, cat.category_name, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS category_spend
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON ...
JOIN order_items oi ON ...
JOIN products p ON ...
JOIN categories cat ON ...
WHERE ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.first_name, cat.category_name, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS category_spend FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id JOIN categories cat ON p.category_id = cat.category_id WHERE o.order_status = 'completed' GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, cat.category_id, cat.category_name ORDER BY category_spend DESC, c.first_name ASC, cat.category_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Spans 5 tables from consumer to product taxonomy to calculate segmented spending totals.
common_mistakes: Omitting category_id or customer_id from GROUP BY.
interview_tip: Multi-table cross-dimensional aggregations are core data warehouse star-schema patterns.
hints: Join the 5 tables sequentially along their foreign keys.

Query: SELECT c.first_name, cat.category_name, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS category_spend FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id JOIN categories cat ON p.category_id = cat.category_id WHERE o.order_status = 'completed' GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, cat.category_id, cat.category_name ORDER BY category_spend DESC, c.first_name ASC, cat.category_name ASC;

title: Calculate Department Project Commitment Hours
description_markdown: Join `departments`, `projects`, and `assignments`. Group by `d.dept_id`, `d.dept_name`, `p.project_id`, and `p.project_name`. Return `d.dept_name`, `p.project_name`, and `SUM(a.hours_worked) AS total_hours`. Order by `total_hours` descending, `d.dept_name` ascending, then `p.project_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Join departments -> projects -> assignments and aggregate
SELECT d.dept_name, p.project_name, SUM(a.hours_worked) AS total_hours
FROM departments d
JOIN projects p ON ...
JOIN assignments a ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, p.project_name, SUM(a.hours_worked) AS total_hours FROM departments d JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id JOIN assignments a ON p.project_id = a.project_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name, p.project_id, p.project_name ORDER BY total_hours DESC, d.dept_name ASC, p.project_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Sums logged labor hours for each project under its owning corporate department.
common_mistakes: Missing p.project_name in GROUP BY.
interview_tip: Group by both primary keys and descriptive names when multiple dimensions are reported.
hints: Query: SELECT d.dept_name, p.project_name, SUM(a.hours_worked) AS total_hours FROM departments d JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id JOIN assignments a ON p.project_id = a.project_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name, p.project_id, p.project_name ORDER BY total_hours DESC, d.dept_name ASC, p.project_name ASC;

title: Tally Student Headcount per Professor Course
description_markdown: Join `professors`, `courses`, and `enrollments`. Group by `p.professor_id`, `p.last_name`, `c.course_id`, and `c.course_name`. Return `p.last_name`, `c.course_name`, and `COUNT(e.student_id) AS student_count`. Order by `student_count` descending, `p.last_name` ascending, then `c.course_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Join professors -> courses -> enrollments and count
SELECT p.last_name, c.course_name, COUNT(e.student_id) AS student_count
FROM professors p
JOIN courses c ON ...
JOIN enrollments e ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT p.last_name, c.course_name, COUNT(e.student_id) AS student_count FROM professors p JOIN courses c ON p.professor_id = c.professor_id JOIN enrollments e ON c.course_id = e.course_id GROUP BY p.professor_id, p.last_name, c.course_id, c.course_name ORDER BY student_count DESC, p.last_name ASC, c.course_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Counts active student enrollment loads per instructor across course offerings.
common_mistakes: Leaving c.course_name out of GROUP BY.
interview_tip: In SQL, include all unaggregated SELECT columns in the GROUP BY clause.
hints: Query: SELECT p.last_name, c.course_name, COUNT(e.student_id) AS student_count FROM professors p JOIN courses c ON p.professor_id = c.professor_id JOIN enrollments e ON c.course_id = e.course_id GROUP BY p.professor_id, p.last_name, c.course_id, c.course_name ORDER BY student_count DESC, p.last_name ASC, c.course_name ASC;

title: Aggregate Sales Revenue by Customer City
description_markdown: Join `customers`, `orders`, and `order_items`. Group by `c.city`. Return `c.city` and `SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS city_revenue`. Order by `city_revenue` descending, then `c.city` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Aggregate city revenue across customers, orders, and items
SELECT c.city, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS city_revenue
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON ...
JOIN order_items oi ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.city, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS city_revenue FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id GROUP BY c.city ORDER BY city_revenue DESC, c.city ASC;
solution_explanation: Aggregates retail purchase volume at the regional city level across transaction items.
common_mistakes: Using SUM(o.total_amount) which can double-count when joining to order_items.
interview_tip: Watch out for fan-out: joining 1 order to 3 items multiplies total_amount by 3 unless calculating at the item level.
hints: Query: SELECT c.city, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS city_revenue FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id GROUP BY c.city ORDER BY city_revenue DESC, c.city ASC;

title: Calculate Total Gross Revenue per Category
description_markdown: Join `categories`, `products`, and `order_items`. Group by `cat.category_id` and `cat.category_name`. Return `cat.category_name` and `SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total_revenue`. Order by `total_revenue` descending, then `cat.category_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Category revenue aggregation
SELECT cat.category_name, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total_revenue
FROM categories cat
JOIN products p ON ...
JOIN order_items oi ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT cat.category_name, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total_revenue FROM categories cat JOIN products p ON cat.category_id = p.category_id JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id GROUP BY cat.category_id, cat.category_name ORDER BY total_revenue DESC, cat.category_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Computes sales revenue rolled up to the category division.
common_mistakes: Grouping solely by category_name.
interview_tip: Group by category_id as well to avoid grouping separate categories that might share names.
hints: Query: SELECT cat.category_name, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS total_revenue FROM categories cat JOIN products p ON cat.category_id = p.category_id JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id GROUP BY cat.category_id, cat.category_name ORDER BY total_revenue DESC, cat.category_name ASC;

title: Calculate Student Overall Assessment Grade Average
description_markdown: Join `students`, `enrollments`, and `marks`. Group by `s.student_id`, `s.first_name`, and `s.last_name`. Return `s.first_name`, `s.last_name`, and `ROUND(AVG(m.score), 2) AS overall_avg_score`. Order by `overall_avg_score` descending, then `s.last_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Student academic score average
SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, ROUND(AVG(m.score), 2) AS overall_avg_score
FROM students s
JOIN enrollments e ON ...
JOIN marks m ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, ROUND(AVG(m.score), 2) AS overall_avg_score FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id JOIN marks m ON e.enrollment_id = m.enrollment_id GROUP BY s.student_id, s.first_name, s.last_name ORDER BY overall_avg_score DESC, s.last_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Aggregates all evaluation scores per student across every course enrollment.
common_mistakes: Forgetting ROUND(..., 2).
interview_tip: Group by student_id, first_name, last_name to satisfy ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY requirements.
hints: Query: SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, ROUND(AVG(m.score), 2) AS overall_avg_score FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id JOIN marks m ON e.enrollment_id = m.enrollment_id GROUP BY s.student_id, s.first_name, s.last_name ORDER BY overall_avg_score DESC, s.last_name ASC;

title: Count Distinct Active Projects Supported per Department Staff
description_markdown: Join `departments`, `employees`, and `assignments`. Group by `d.dept_id` and `d.dept_name`. Return `d.dept_name` and `COUNT(DISTINCT a.project_id) AS active_projects_supported`. Order by `active_projects_supported` descending, then `d.dept_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Count distinct projects supported per department
SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(DISTINCT a.project_id) AS active_projects_supported
FROM departments d
JOIN employees e ON ...
JOIN assignments a ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(DISTINCT a.project_id) AS active_projects_supported FROM departments d JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY active_projects_supported DESC, d.dept_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Measures project cross-staffing by counting unique projects worked by department personnel.
common_mistakes: Leaving off DISTINCT in COUNT(a.project_id), causing inflated counts when multiple employees work the same project.
interview_tip: In many-to-many multi-table joins, always use COUNT(DISTINCT id) to eliminate duplicate matches.
hints: Query: SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(DISTINCT a.project_id) AS active_projects_supported FROM departments d JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY active_projects_supported DESC, d.dept_name ASC;

title: Aggregate Order Count and Units Sold by Country
description_markdown: Join `customers`, `orders`, and `order_items`. Group by `c.country`. Return `c.country`, `COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS total_orders`, and `SUM(oi.quantity) AS total_units`. Order by `total_orders` descending, then `c.country` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Country order and unit aggregations
SELECT c.country, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS total_orders, SUM(oi.quantity) AS total_units
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON ...
JOIN order_items oi ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.country, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS total_orders, SUM(oi.quantity) AS total_units FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id GROUP BY c.country ORDER BY total_orders DESC, c.country ASC;
solution_explanation: Avoids fan-out duplication on order count by applying COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) across item rows.
common_mistakes: Using COUNT(o.order_id) without DISTINCT, which counts the line items rather than unique orders.
interview_tip: This is a quintessential multi-table fan-out trap: joining parent to child multiplies parent rows.
hints: Use `COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS total_orders` and `SUM(oi.quantity) AS total_units`.

Query: SELECT c.country, COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id) AS total_orders, SUM(oi.quantity) AS total_units FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id GROUP BY c.country ORDER BY total_orders DESC, c.country ASC;

title: Count Distinct Payment Methods Utilized per Customer
description_markdown: Join `customers`, `orders`, and `payments`. Group by `c.customer_id` and `c.first_name`. Return `c.first_name` and `COUNT(DISTINCT pay.payment_method) AS distinct_methods_used`. Order by `distinct_methods_used` descending, then `c.first_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Distinct payment methods per customer
SELECT c.first_name, COUNT(DISTINCT pay.payment_method) AS distinct_methods_used
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON ...
JOIN payments pay ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.first_name, COUNT(DISTINCT pay.payment_method) AS distinct_methods_used FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN payments pay ON o.order_id = pay.order_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name ORDER BY distinct_methods_used DESC, c.first_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Analyzes payment diversity across consumer profiles by traversing orders to payment entries.
common_mistakes: Forgetting DISTINCT in COUNT.
interview_tip: Customers who use multiple tender types (credit card, paypal, apple pay) have different checkout conversion characteristics.
hints: Query: SELECT c.first_name, COUNT(DISTINCT pay.payment_method) AS distinct_methods_used FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN payments pay ON o.order_id = pay.order_id GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name ORDER BY distinct_methods_used DESC, c.first_name ASC;

title: Calculate Department Average Project Assignment Rating
description_markdown: Join `departments`, `projects`, and `assignments`. Group by `d.dept_id` and `d.dept_name`. Return `d.dept_name` and `ROUND(AVG(a.rating), 2) AS avg_project_rating`. Order by `avg_project_rating` descending, then `d.dept_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Department average assignment rating
SELECT d.dept_name, ROUND(AVG(a.rating), 2) AS avg_project_rating
FROM departments d
JOIN projects p ON ...
JOIN assignments a ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, ROUND(AVG(a.rating), 2) AS avg_project_rating FROM departments d JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id JOIN assignments a ON p.project_id = a.project_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY avg_project_rating DESC, d.dept_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Measures project delivery quality at the department executive level.
common_mistakes: Rounding to 1 decimal place instead of 2.
interview_tip: Always round float aggregates to 2 decimals for test comparison stability.
hints: Query: SELECT d.dept_name, ROUND(AVG(a.rating), 2) AS avg_project_rating FROM departments d JOIN projects p ON d.dept_id = p.dept_id JOIN assignments a ON p.project_id = a.project_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY avg_project_rating DESC, d.dept_name ASC;

title: Calculate Total Completed Academic Credits Earned
description_markdown: Join `students`, `enrollments`, and `courses`. Filter for completed courses where `e.status = 'completed'`. Group by `s.student_id`, `s.first_name`, and `s.last_name`. Return `s.first_name`, `s.last_name`, and `SUM(c.credits) AS total_credits_earned`. Order by `total_credits_earned` descending, then `s.last_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Student credits earned from completed courses
SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, SUM(c.credits) AS total_credits_earned
FROM students s
JOIN enrollments e ON ...
JOIN courses c ON ...
WHERE ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, SUM(c.credits) AS total_credits_earned FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id JOIN courses c ON e.course_id = c.course_id WHERE e.status = 'completed' GROUP BY s.student_id, s.first_name, s.last_name ORDER BY total_credits_earned DESC, s.last_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Tallies academic progress by summing course credits for successfully passed classes.
common_mistakes: Including dropped courses in the credit sum.
interview_tip: Filtering status = 'completed' ensures non-credit attempts are excluded before aggregation.
hints: Query: SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, SUM(c.credits) AS total_credits_earned FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id JOIN courses c ON e.course_id = c.course_id WHERE e.status = 'completed' GROUP BY s.student_id, s.first_name, s.last_name ORDER BY total_credits_earned DESC, s.last_name ASC;

title: Reconcile Product Review Activity with Order Frequency
description_markdown: Perform a `LEFT JOIN` from `products` to `reviews` on `p.product_id = r.product_id`, and a `LEFT JOIN` from `products` to `order_items` on `p.product_id = oi.product_id`. Group by `p.product_id` and `p.product_name`. Return `p.product_name`, `COUNT(DISTINCT r.review_id) AS review_count`, and `COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS order_count`. Order by `order_count` descending, `review_count` descending, then `p.product_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Reconcile reviews and orders for products
SELECT p.product_name, COUNT(DISTINCT r.review_id) AS review_count, COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS order_count
FROM products p
LEFT JOIN reviews r ON ...
LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON ...
GROUP BY ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT p.product_name, COUNT(DISTINCT r.review_id) AS review_count, COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS order_count FROM products p LEFT JOIN reviews r ON p.product_id = r.product_id LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name ORDER BY order_count DESC, review_count DESC, p.product_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Joining two separate 1-to-many child tables to the same parent table creates a Cartesian fan-out across children; using COUNT(DISTINCT) fixes the resulting product duplication.
common_mistakes: Using COUNT(r.review_id) without DISTINCT, which would be multiplied by the number of order_items.
interview_tip: This is the classic Cartesian chasm problem when joining multiple one-to-many child tables in a single query.
hints: Join `reviews` and `order_items` using `LEFT JOIN` to preserve zero-activity products.

Query: SELECT p.product_name, COUNT(DISTINCT r.review_id) AS review_count, COUNT(DISTINCT oi.order_id) AS order_count FROM products p LEFT JOIN reviews r ON p.product_id = r.product_id LEFT JOIN order_items oi ON p.product_id = oi.product_id GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name ORDER BY order_count DESC, review_count DESC, p.product_name ASC;

title: Filter High-Value Customer Purchases by Category
description_markdown: Join `customers`, `orders`, `order_items`, `products`, and `categories`. Filter for completed orders (`o.order_status = 'completed'`). Group by `c.customer_id`, `c.first_name`, `cat.category_id`, and `cat.category_name`. Filter with `HAVING SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) >= 400.00`. Return `c.first_name`, `cat.category_name`, and `SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS category_spend`. Order by `category_spend` descending, then `c.first_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- 5-table join with HAVING filter
SELECT c.first_name, cat.category_name, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS category_spend
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON ...
JOIN order_items oi ON ...
JOIN products p ON ...
JOIN categories cat ON ...
WHERE ...
GROUP BY ...
HAVING ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT c.first_name, cat.category_name, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS category_spend FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id JOIN categories cat ON p.category_id = cat.category_id WHERE o.order_status = 'completed' GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, cat.category_id, cat.category_name HAVING SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) >= 400.00 ORDER BY category_spend DESC, c.first_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Combines 5-table join resolution with aggregate HAVING filtering to identify high-spending customer category niches.
common_mistakes: Placing the aggregate spend condition in WHERE.
interview_tip: WHERE operates on raw rows before grouping; HAVING filters aggregated cohorts.
hints: Join the 5 tables through the customer -> order -> item -> product -> category pipeline.

Query: SELECT c.first_name, cat.category_name, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) AS category_spend FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id JOIN order_items oi ON o.order_id = oi.order_id JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.product_id JOIN categories cat ON p.category_id = cat.category_id WHERE o.order_status = 'completed' GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.first_name, cat.category_id, cat.category_name HAVING SUM(oi.quantity * oi.unit_price) >= 400.00 ORDER BY category_spend DESC, c.first_name ASC;

title: Identify Star Project Roles Across Departments
description_markdown: Join `departments`, `employees`, `assignments`, and `projects`. Filter for assignments where `a.rating >= 4.8`. Return `d.dept_name`, `e.first_name`, `p.project_name`, `a.role`, and `a.rating`. Order by `a.rating` descending, `d.dept_name` ascending, `e.first_name` ascending, then `p.project_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- 4-table join on department staff and high-rated projects
SELECT d.dept_name, e.first_name, p.project_name, a.role, a.rating
FROM departments d
JOIN employees e ON ...
JOIN assignments a ON ...
JOIN projects p ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT d.dept_name, e.first_name, p.project_name, a.role, a.rating FROM departments d JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id JOIN projects p ON a.project_id = p.project_id WHERE a.rating >= 4.8 ORDER BY a.rating DESC, d.dept_name ASC, e.first_name ASC, p.project_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Highlights top individual contributors and their projects across corporate departmental boundaries.
common_mistakes: Joining projects on d.dept_id instead of a.project_id.
interview_tip: Keep the join path linear: departments -> employees -> assignments -> projects.
hints: Query: SELECT d.dept_name, e.first_name, p.project_name, a.role, a.rating FROM departments d JOIN employees e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id JOIN assignments a ON e.emp_id = a.emp_id JOIN projects p ON a.project_id = p.project_id WHERE a.rating >= 4.8 ORDER BY a.rating DESC, d.dept_name ASC, e.first_name ASC, p.project_name ASC;

title: Identify Dean's List Students on Final Assessments
description_markdown: Join `students`, `enrollments`, `courses`, and `marks`. Filter where `m.assessment_type = 'final'` and `m.score >= 95.00`. Return `s.first_name`, `s.last_name`, `c.course_name`, and `m.score`. Order by `m.score` descending, `s.last_name` ascending, then `c.course_name` ascending.
starter_query:
-- 4-table join for Dean's list final exams
SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, c.course_name, m.score
FROM students s
JOIN enrollments e ON ...
JOIN courses c ON ...
JOIN marks m ON ...
WHERE ...
ORDER BY ...;
solution_query: SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, c.course_name, m.score FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id JOIN courses c ON e.course_id = c.course_id JOIN marks m ON e.enrollment_id = m.enrollment_id WHERE m.assessment_type = 'final' AND m.score >= 95.00 ORDER BY m.score DESC, s.last_name ASC, c.course_name ASC;
solution_explanation: Reconciles student academic records across courses and evaluations to identify highest academic honors.

interview_tip: Combining multi-table joins with multiple WHERE filters tests complete mastery of SQL query structure.
hints: Query: SELECT s.first_name, s.last_name, c.course_name, m.score FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.student_id = e.student_id JOIN courses c ON e.course_id = c.course_id JOIN marks m ON e.enrollment_id = m.enrollment_id WHERE m.assessment_type = 'final' AND m.score >= 95.00 ORDER BY m.score DESC, s.last_name ASC, c.course_name ASC;
